questionEnglish: According to the autobiographical account 'At the High School', what were the specific birth and death years of Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi?
explanation: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was born in the year 1869 and passed away in the year 1948, as indicated in the biographical brief of the lesson.

questionEnglish: From which larger literary masterpiece by Mahatma Gandhi has the selection 'At the High School' been directly extracted?
options: Hind Swaraj or Indian Home Rule
The Story of My Experiments with Truth
The Satyagraha in South Africa
Key to Health
answer: The Story of My Experiments with Truth
explanation: The prose piece 'At the High School' is an excerpt from Mahatma Gandhi's famous autobiography titled 'The Story of My Experiments with Truth'.

questionEnglish: How did young Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi evaluate his own intellectual capabilities or academic talents during his time at the high school?
options: He believed he possessed exceptional genius and intellectual superiority.
He did not have a high regard for his own ability and was surprised by his achievements.
He assumed he was entirely incompetent and bound to fail every examination.
He expected praise and special treatment from all his subject instructors.
answer: He did not have a high regard for his own ability and was surprised by his achievements.
explanation: Gandhi writes that he never held a high opinion of his own intellectual capability, which is why winning prizes and educational scholarships always astonished him.

questionEnglish: What was Gandhi's genuine reaction whenever he unexpectedly won school prizes or academic merit scholarships?
options: He felt immense arrogance and look down upon his classmates.
He was filled with utter astonishment and wonder at his success.
He expressed extreme dissatisfaction and demanded higher amounts.
He considered it an ordinary matter that required no emotional reaction.
answer: He was filled with utter astonishment and wonder at his success.
explanation: As stated in the text, Gandhi was astonished whenever he won prizes and scholarships because he didn't rate his own skills very highly.

questionEnglish: At which point in his high school journey did Gandhi initially begin to win institutional prizes?
options: After passing out of the second standard
During his very first term in the first standard
Only after completing his matriculation exams
When he shifted to a school in England
answer: After passing out of the second standard
explanation: In his account, Gandhi explicitly records that he won prizes after he successfully passed out of the second standard.

questionEnglish: In which school standards did Gandhi successfully secure merit scholarships of rupees four and rupees ten respectively?
options: In the third and fourth standards
In the fifth and sixth standards
In the second and fifth standards
In the fourth and seventh standards
answer: In the fifth and sixth standards
explanation: The text confirms that Gandhi obtained scholarships of four rupees and ten rupees in the fifth and sixth standards respectively.

questionEnglish: To what factor did Gandhi largely attribute his success in obtaining school scholarships rather than his personal brilliance?
options: To his absolute mastery over difficult arithmetic problems
To good fortune and the fact that the scholarships were reserved for Sorath boys
To intense lobbying and political interference by his parents
To the total absence of other students in his senior classes
answer: To good fortune and the fact that the scholarships were reserved for Sorath boys
explanation: Gandhi modestly explains that his scholarships were due more to good luck, as they were meant for students coming from the Sorath region of Kathiawad.

questionEnglish: How did the high school authorities keep Gandhi's parents informed regarding his annual behavioral conduct and academic progress?
options: By publishing monthly progress reports in the local newspaper
By sending formal certificates of progress and character to them every year
By requesting mandatory weekly face-to-face guardian conferences
By writing urgent telegraphs only when he committed serious errors
answer: By sending formal certificates of progress and character to them every year
explanation: The high school had a regular practice of sending official certificates of progress and character to the parents on an annual basis.

questionEnglish: What positive observation did Gandhi make regarding the annual certificates sent by the school to his home?
options: They frequently warned his family about his poor attendance.
He never received a bad certificate, and his progress was always praised.
They showed that he was a champion player in football matches.
They contained complaints from his strict Sanskrit teacher.
answer: He never received a bad certificate, and his progress was always praised.
explanation: Gandhi writes with satisfaction that he never had a bad certificate sent home, and his teachers consistently showed affection toward him.

questionEnglish: What personal attribute did young Gandhi guard with extreme jealousy and intense care during his high school days?
options: His position as the primary monitor of his class
His collection of expensive English literature textbooks
His moral character and personal conduct
His record time in running the hundred-meter race
answer: His moral character and personal conduct
explanation: Gandhi states in his autobiography that he very jealously guarded his character, as any moral slip was deeply disturbing to him.

questionEnglish: What physical or emotional reaction did Gandhi exhibit whenever there was the least little blemish on his moral character?
options: He would burst into tears and experience deep mental anguish.
He would argue aggressively to prove his teachers wrong.
He would run away from the school premises immediately.
He would laugh it off as an insignificant mistake.
answer: He would burst into tears and experience deep mental anguish.
explanation: The text states that the least little blemish on his character drew tears from his eyes, showing how deeply sensitive he was to moral integrity.

questionEnglish: Why was receiving a formal rebuke or reprimand from a teacher completely unbearable for young Gandhi?
options: Because it resulted in immediate expulsion from the classroom
Because he felt deeply pained by the idea of being unworthy or causing disapproval
Because it meant he would lose his monthly monetary scholarship
Because his friends would tease him continuously during the recess
answer: Because he felt deeply pained by the idea of being unworthy or causing disapproval
explanation: Gandhi found a rebuke unbearable because it implied that he had done something wrong or shameful, which deeply hurt his conscience.

questionEnglish: When Gandhi received physical corporal punishment in his school, what aspect of the incident pained him the most?
options: The severe physical bruising on his hands
The heavy monetary penalty that accompanied the punishment
The realization that his action was viewed as a deserved punishment
The fact that his brother laughed at his situation
answer: The realization that his action was viewed as a deserved punishment
explanation: Gandhi records that he did not mind the physical pain of the punishment as much as the agonizing fact that he was deemed to have deserved it.

questionEnglish: Who was the Headmaster of the high school during Gandhi’s senior educational years, described as a popular but strict figure?
options: Mr. Giles
Mr. Dorabji Edulji Gimi
Mr. Krishnashankar Pandya
Mr. Karamchand Gandhi
answer: Mr. Dorabji Edulji Gimi
explanation: The strict, methodical, and disciplined headmaster of the school during Gandhi's senior years was Mr. Dorabji Edulji Gimi.

questionEnglish: What specific set of activities did the Headmaster, Mr. Gimi, make mandatory for all the senior boys of the upper standards?
options: Sanskrit translation and calligraphic practice
Gymnastics and cricket physical exercises
Debate competitions and public speaking courses
Manual farming and structural carpentry
answer: Gymnastics and cricket physical exercises
explanation: Mr. Dorabji Edulji Gimi made gymnastics and cricket compulsory for all senior boys in the upper standards of the school.

questionEnglish: What was young Gandhi’s immediate personal attitude toward the mandatory sports activities introduced by the Headmaster?
options: He was thrilled and immediately volunteered to lead the cricket team.
He disliked both gymnastics and cricket intensely and avoided them.
He preferred gymnastics but strongly despised playing cricket.
He requested extra classes to perfect his sporting skills.
answer: He disliked both gymnastics and cricket intensely and avoided them.
explanation: Gandhi explicitly notes, 'I disliked both. I never took part in any exercise, cricket or football, before they were made compulsory.'

questionEnglish: What psychological and social factor was a major reason for Gandhi’s aloofness from all school games and physical activities before they became compulsory?
options: His extreme constitutional shyness and fear of social interactions
His continuous physical illnesses and asthma attacks
His intellectual pride which made him look down on sportsmen
His inability to purchase the uniform required for sports
answer: His extreme constitutional shyness and fear of social interactions
explanation: The text states that Gandhi's constitutional shyness, which made him avoid company, was a primary reason for his aloofness from sports.

questionEnglish: What false notion or incorrect intellectual belief did young Gandhi hold regarding physical training and school education?
options: That sports should only be practiced by students who fail exams
That gymnastics had absolutely nothing to do with formal education
That playing games would permanently damage a student's eyesight
That physical training was only meant for military cadets
answer: That gymnastics had absolutely nothing to do with formal education
explanation: Gandhi confesses that he held a false notion during his school days that physical exercise had no proper connection with real education.

questionEnglish: What mature understanding did Gandhi eventually develop later in life regarding the position of physical training in a school curriculum?
options: It should replace all textbook reading entirely.
It should have as much place in the curriculum as intellectual or mental training.
It should only be taught as an optional subject over weekends.
It should be reserved purely for students with poor mental capabilities.
answer: It should have as much place in the curriculum as intellectual or mental training.
explanation: Later in life, Gandhi realized that physical training is just as crucial as mental training in forming a balanced, well-rounded individual.

questionEnglish: Apart from his deep shyness, what urgent domestic responsibility made Gandhi desperately wish to avoid the compulsory gymnastics classes?
options: His obligation to run his family's local commercial shop
His intense desire to nurse and serve his ailing, bedridden father
His personal routine of practicing religious chants at home
His commitment to teaching reading skills to neighborhood children
answer: His intense desire to nurse and serve his ailing, bedridden father
explanation: Gandhi wanted to rush home immediately after school hours to serve as a nurse to his sick father, which created a direct conflict with after-school gymnastics.

questionEnglish: On which particular day of the week did the famous cloud incident occur, leading to Gandhi being falsely accused of lying about missing gymnastics?
options: On a rainy Monday morning
On a busy Friday afternoon
On a Saturday afternoon when school closed early
On a Sunday when a special session was called
answer: On a Saturday afternoon when school closed early
explanation: The incident occurred on a Saturday afternoon when school had wrapped up early, and the boys had to return at 4:00 PM for gymnastics.

questionEnglish: Why did Gandhi fail to arrive at the high school playing field at the exact appointed time for his Saturday gymnastics class?
options: He was intentionally hiding to avoid the strict instructor.
He had no watch, and the heavily overcast clouds deceived him regarding the correct time.
He got lost on his way back from the local city market.
His father forcibly locked him inside his room to prevent him from playing.
answer: He had no watch, and the heavily overcast clouds deceived him regarding the correct time.
explanation: Gandhi explains that he did not own a watch, and the cloudy weather made it difficult to gauge the time accurately, causing him to arrive late.

questionEnglish: What did Headmaster Mr. Gimi discover when he strictly examined the school attendance roll the day after the Saturday gymnastics session?
options: That Gandhi had secured the highest rank in physical agility
That Gandhi was marked completely absent from the mandatory class
That someone else had fraudulently signed the roll for Gandhi
That the sports instructor had misplaced the entire registry
answer: That Gandhi was marked completely absent from the mandatory class
explanation: Upon reviewing the attendance sheets the next morning, the Headmaster discovered that Gandhi was marked down as absent.

questionEnglish: What disciplinary action did Mr. Gimi take against Gandhi when he refused to believe the story about the deceptive clouds?
options: He expelled Gandhi from the high school for the entire term.
He ordered Gandhi to pay a penalty fine of one or two annas.
He forced Gandhi to run ten laps around the cricket field.
He sent a formal notice to the local police department.
answer: He ordered Gandhi to pay a penalty fine of one or two annas.
explanation: Refusing to accept Gandhi's explanation, Mr. Gimi penalized him by ordering him to pay a fine of one or two annas.

questionEnglish: What specific moral distress or emotional agony did Gandhi suffer as a direct result of Mr. Gimi's disciplinary fine?
options: He was deeply pained by the fact that he was convicted of lying.
He felt distressed because he had no money to purchase his evening meal.
He was worried that his future entry into college was permanently blocked.
He felt ashamed that his friends would no longer talk to him.
answer: He was deeply pained by the fact that he was convicted of lying.
explanation: The fact that his true story was rejected and he was branded a liar was deeply painful to Gandhi's sense of honesty.

questionEnglish: What vital life-lesson did Gandhi extract from his traumatic experience of being penalized for an accidental absence?
options: That a student should never trust any headmaster under any condition
That a person dedicated to truth must also be a person of care and alertness
That rainy days are completely unsuited for academic progress
That physical education should be avoided by honest individuals
answer: That a person dedicated to truth must also be a person of care and alertness
explanation: Gandhi writes, 'I saw that a man of truth must also be a man of care,' highlighting that carelessness can inadvertently compromise one's reputation for truth.

questionEnglish: How did the dispute regarding Gandhi's compulsory gymnastics attendance finally reach a complete resolution?
options: Gandhi chose to leave the school and study at home.
The fine was remitted, and his father secured an official exemption via a letter to the headmaster.
The sports teacher apologized directly to Gandhi's family.
Gandhi decided to skip all future classes and accept the consequences.
answer: The fine was remitted, and his father secured an official exemption via a letter to the headmaster.
explanation: Gandhi managed to get the fine canceled, and his father sent a written request to the headmaster ensuring his full exemption so he could serve at home.

questionEnglish: What was young Gandhi’s initial view regarding the importance of good handwriting in a regular school curriculum?
options: He believed it was the single most vital element of academic success.
He nurtured a mistaken notion that good handwriting was not a necessary part of education.
He assumed that only artists and painters needed to practice handwriting.
He thought that bad handwriting was a unique sign of high intellect.
answer: He nurtured a mistaken notion that good handwriting was not a necessary part of education.
explanation: Gandhi states that during his school days, he held the incorrect view that having beautiful handwriting was not an essential aspect of proper schooling.

questionEnglish: Where did Gandhi finally realize his grave mistake regarding the lifelong neglect of his personal handwriting style?
options: When he joined his primary school at Porbandar
When he traveled to England and later practiced law in South Africa
When he sat for his final geography matriculation paper
When he was teaching young kids in his own ashram
answer: When he traveled to England and later practiced law in South Africa
explanation: It was only when he arrived in England and later saw the pristine, beautiful handwriting of young lawyers in South Africa that he deeply repented his poor penmanship.

questionEnglish: What sight in South Africa made Gandhi feel profoundly ashamed and filled with deep repentance regarding his own handwriting?
options: The beautifully calligraphed official maps of the African continent
The exceptional and beautiful handwriting of young lawyers and public officials born there
The complex mathematical diagrams drawn on court blackboards
The highly stylized printed typography of local legal books
answer: The exceptional and beautiful handwriting of young lawyers and public officials born there
explanation: Seeing the elegant handwriting of professionals in South Africa made him recognize how messy his own writing was by comparison.

questionEnglish: Based on his personal reflections, how did Gandhi define bad or unformed handwriting later in his life?
options: As an indicator of a rapid and highly creative mindset
As a clear sign of an imperfect and incomplete education
As a minor technical flaw that can be easily overlooked
As a unique characteristic of individuals who master science
answer: As a clear sign of an imperfect and incomplete education
explanation: Gandhi states clearly in the text: 'I saw that bad handwriting should be regarded as a sign of an imperfect education.'

questionEnglish: What pedagogic method does Gandhi recommend for children to ensure they develop beautiful handwriting naturally?
options: They should be forced to copy lengthy print essays from a very young age.
They should be taught the art of drawing objects first before learning to form alphabet letters.
They should use typing machines before handling ink pens.
They should avoid writing until they completely master verbal speech.
answer: They should be taught the art of drawing objects first before learning to form alphabet letters.
explanation: Gandhi suggests that children should first learn to draw things like birds and flowers, so they treat forming letters as an artistic exercise rather than a chore.

questionEnglish: Why did Gandhi find the study of the Sanskrit language much more difficult and stressful than geometry?
options: Because the Sanskrit classroom was situated in a damp basement
Because he felt that everything in Sanskrit had to be thoroughly memorized by heart
Because the Sanskrit language had no alphabet characters
Because his father strictly forbade him from learning religious terms
answer: Because he felt that everything in Sanskrit had to be thoroughly memorized by heart
explanation: Gandhi notes that while geometry relied on logical reasoning, Sanskrit required extensive memorization of rules and text, which he found difficult.

questionEnglish: In which particular class or standard of his high school did the formal teaching of Sanskrit begin?
options: The first standard
The second standard
The fourth standard
The seventh standard
answer: The fourth standard
explanation: The text notes that Sanskrit was introduced as a compulsory course starting from the fourth standard.

questionEnglish: What change occurred when Gandhi entered the sixth standard that left him feeling completely disheartened with Sanskrit?
options: The school doubled the number of Sanskrit books.
The Sanskrit teacher proved to be an extremely demanding and rigid taskmaster.
He lost his favorite vocabulary notebook.
The course was altered to focus entirely on difficult calculations.
answer: The Sanskrit teacher proved to be an extremely demanding and rigid taskmaster.
explanation: Upon entering the sixth standard, Gandhi felt discouraged because the Sanskrit teacher was very strict and put a lot of pressure on the boys.

questionEnglish: What kind of underlying professional dynamic or environment existed between the school's Sanskrit and Persian teachers?
options: They shared a deep familial relationship as brothers.
There was a sort of silent rivalry going on between them.
They jointly conducted classes in the same large hall.
They were constantly planning to quit the institution together.
answer: There was a sort of silent rivalry going on between them.
explanation: The text states that there was a subtle rivalry between the two language instructors regarding their respective classes.

questionEnglish: What rumor or popular opinion circulated among the students regarding the Persian class and its teacher?
options: That Persian was incredibly difficult and required advanced skills
That Persian was very easy and the teacher was lenient and considerate
That the Persian teacher regularly handed out severe punishments
That Persian was only intended for foreign students
answer: That Persian was very easy and the teacher was lenient and considerate
explanation: The boys often chatted among themselves that Persian was simple to master and that the Persian teacher was remarkably kind and easygoing.

questionEnglish: Tempted by the widespread talk of its simplicity, what impulsive action did Gandhi take one day in school?
options: He skipped school to watch a sports match.
He went and sat down among the students in the Persian class.
He openly challenged the Headmaster during assembly.
He demanded a transfer to another high school in Rajkot.
answer: He went and sat down among the students in the Persian class.
explanation: Lured by the idea that Persian was easier, Gandhi walked into the Persian classroom one day and sat down to take the lesson.

questionEnglish: How did the Sanskrit teacher respond to finding out that Gandhi had abandoned his class for the Persian section?
options: He ignored Gandhi's choice and removed his name from the records.
He was deeply grieved, called Gandhi to his side, and spoke to him with affection.
He immediately fined Gandhi a heavy penalty of five rupees.
He burst into anger and shouted at Gandhi in front of the school.
answer: He was deeply grieved, called Gandhi to his side, and spoke to him with affection.
explanation: The Sanskrit teacher was saddened by Gandhi's departure. He kindly called Gandhi over to explain why he should not give up on his roots.

questionEnglish: What deeply cultural and religious point did the Sanskrit teacher use to touch Gandhi's conscience?
options: He explained that Sanskrit was the sacred language of Gandhi's own religion and family.
He mentioned that Persian would soon be banned from the regional syllabus.
He promised that he would give Gandhi full marks without any exams.
He stated that learning Sanskrit would make him a wealthy lawyer.
answer: He explained that Sanskrit was the sacred language of Gandhi's own religion and family.
explanation: The teacher reminded Gandhi that he was a son of a Vaishnava family and that Sanskrit was the language of his faith, full of profound wisdom.

questionEnglish: How did the Sanskrit teacher's gentle and affectionate treatment ultimately alter Gandhi's academic course?
options: It made Gandhi double his resolve to master Persian.
He could not disregard the teacher's earnest affection and went back to Sanskrit.
He decided to drop both languages entirely from his studies.
He complained to his father about the teacher's emotional talk.
answer: He could not disregard the teacher's earnest affection and went back to Sanskrit.
explanation: The genuine kindness shown by the teacher touched Gandhi deeply, making it impossible for him to turn away, so he returned to the Sanskrit class.

questionEnglish: How did Gandhi view his youthful decision to listen to his Sanskrit teacher later during his adult life?
options: He deeply regretted it because it wasted his valuable hours.
He remembered the teacher with gratitude because it allowed him to appreciate sacred Indian texts.
He thought it was an insignificant event that had no impact on his life.
He felt that he should have chosen Persian instead to help his career.
answer: He remembered the teacher with gratitude because it allowed him to appreciate sacred Indian texts.
explanation: Gandhi notes that he always look back at the incident with gratitude, as the foundational Sanskrit he kept learning enabled him to read sacred books later in life.

questionEnglish: What is the exact definition of the term 'autobiography' as contextualized by Mahatma Gandhi’s textbook chapter?
options: A historical biography written about a famous leader by a contemporary writer
The written account of a person's life history composed directly by that person themselves
A collection of fictional short stories based on actual village events
An official school progress report published by a state board
answer: The written account of a person's life history composed directly by that person themselves
explanation: An autobiography is a self-written account of one's own life, just as 'The Story of My Experiments with Truth' was written by Gandhi himself.

questionEnglish: In the phrase 'I very jealously guarded my character', what does the adverb 'jealously' mean in this context?
options: Feeling envious and bitter towards the successes of others
With extreme, watchful care and protective vigilance
In a highly aggressive, angry, and destructive manner
Secretly and dishonestly out of fear of detection
answer: With extreme, watchful care and protective vigilance
explanation: In this text, 'jealously' means protecting something very carefully and fiercely to ensure it remains clean and unblemished.

questionEnglish: What does the expression 'it was considered my desert' reveal about Gandhi's feelings regarding his punishment?
options: He believed he was being abandoned in a hot, dry wasteland.
He felt that the teacher viewed the punishment as something he fully deserved.
He assumed he was receiving a sweet reward at the end of the class.
He thought the punishment was a completely illegal action.
answer: He felt that the teacher viewed the punishment as something he fully deserved.
explanation: The term 'desert' (pronounced dih-zurt) in this older literary context refers to what one deserves, whether a reward or a punishment.

questionEnglish: What was the name of the educational supervisor who tested the spellings of Gandhi's class using five specific English words?
options: Mr. Gimi
Mr. Giles
Mr. Pandya
Mr. Alexander
answer: Mr. Giles
explanation: The school inspector who conducted the spelling test where Gandhi made an error was named Mr. Giles.

questionEnglish: How did Gandhi's teacher try to assist him during the spelling inspection when he noticed the misspelled word 'Kettle'?
options: He whispered the correct spelling directly into Gandhi's ear.
He tried to prompt Gandhi with the point of his boot to copy from his neighbor's slate.
He took Gandhi's slate away and corrected it using his own chalk.
He simple ignored Gandhi's mistake and moved to the next row.
answer: He tried to prompt Gandhi with the point of his boot to copy from his neighbor's slate.
explanation: The teacher used his boot to subtly gesture or prompt Gandhi to copy the correct spelling from the student sitting next to him.

questionEnglish: What internal conviction stopped Gandhi from following his class teacher’s physical prompts to copy during the exam?
options: He thought his neighbor’s spelling was also completely wrong.
He firmly believed that teachers were meant to prevent copying, not encourage it.
He was too proud to take any assistance from a classmate.
He could not see the neighbor's slate due to poor lighting.
answer: He firmly believed that teachers were meant to prevent copying, not encourage it.
explanation: Gandhi's simple moral framework could not comprehend a teacher encouraging cheating, as he believed teachers were there to enforce honesty.

questionEnglish: What quality of Gandhi’s mind is illuminated by his complete inability to find fault with his elders or teachers despite their visible flaws?
options: A total lack of normal critical thinking skills
An innate, deep-seated reverence and respect for authority figures and elders
A desire to look stupid so that he could escape difficult exams
An underlying plan to secure favor from his school headmaster
answer: An innate, deep-seated reverence and respect for authority figures and elders
explanation: Gandhi notes that he naturally lacked the capacity to detect flaws in his teachers or elders, showcasing his deep moral respect for them.

questionEnglish: What does the text highlight as the ultimate lesson to be drawn from Gandhi’s reflection on school curricula?
options: Intellectual studies must completely override physical sports activities.
A true and complete education requires the harmonious development of both body and mind.
Learning multiple languages is completely unnecessary for a regular career.
One should focus exclusively on arts subjects like drawing and painting.
answer: A true and complete education requires the harmonious development of both body and mind.
explanation: Gandhi's combined reflections on gymnastics and academic learning demonstrate that both physical and mental training are vital parts of an ideal education.
